sentences.text: Dreadnoughtus schrani is the only species within the genus Dreadnoughtus, a name given by Kenneth Lacovara and colleagues in 2014.
This animal was a titanosaurian sauropod, a group of giant plant-eating dinosaurs, and its skeleton offers unique details about the limbs and shoulder and hip structures of these giants.
The single known individual stood approximately 26 meters long and reached a height of about 12.8 meters, making it roughly two stories tall.
Fossils representing 45.3 percent of the estimated total number of bones make up the known skeleton.
The immature type specimen measured 26 meters in length and weighed between 48 and 49 metric tons, representing one of the largest dinosaurs known from well-preserved skeletons.
Its pelvic bone, the ilium, measured 1.31 meters in length, a dimension larger than that of any other known dinosaur.
The scapula measured 1.74 meters, exceeding the length of any known titanosaur scapula, while the forearm was also longer than previously known for any titanosaur.
American paleontologist Kenneth Lacovara discovered the remains in 2005 in Patagonia, Argentina, and the species was formally described in 2014 from fossils found in the Cerro Fortaleza Formation.
Two partial skeletons were unearthed in the Cerro Fortaleza Formation in Santa Cruz Province, dating to approximately 76 to 70 million years ago.
To study the bones in detail, researchers utilized a NextEngine 3D laser scanner to create digital models of both specimens.
In 2022, soft tissues and collagens were discovered within the holotype specimen, the specific individual the species is based on.
Evidence indicates the holotype was not fully grown when it died, a finding supported by a 2014 study showing both specimens were immature and still growing.
This immaturity may explain the discrepancies found between different mass estimation methods used by scientists.
The specimens likely died and were buried rapidly during a flood caused by a river levee break.
Small theropod teeth found near the bones suggest scavenging, possibly by megaraptorans like Orkoraptor.
Paleontologist Kenneth Lacovara compared the animal's gait to that of an Imperial Walker.
